```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7.2,
  fig.height = 5.4,
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 96
```

Diplomacy is a game of negotiation played on a map of Europe as it stood
before the First World War. Seven Great Powers share 75 provinces, 34 of
which are supply centres; a power that comes to control 18 of those centres
wins outright. There are no dice. Every player writes orders for every one of
their units in secret, all the orders are revealed at once, and a single set
of rules decides what actually happened.

That last step is the hard part, and it is what this package is mostly about.
`diplomacyR` gives you the board, an adjudicator that resolves a turn under
the standard rules, a phase machine that carries a game from Spring 1901 to
its conclusion, a handful of bots, and the tools to simulate and analyse many
games at once.

```{r library}
library(diplomacyR)
```

## The board

`dp_map()` loads the standard seven-power board. It is a validated object,
not a bare list: the province table, the army and fleet adjacency graphs, the
supply centres, the home centres and the canonical opening position all
travel together.

```{r map}
board <- dp_map()
board
```

Provinces are addressed by three-letter codes. `dp_provinces()` lists them,
optionally filtered by type.

```{r provinces}
head(dp_provinces(board, type = "sea"), 5)
```

Armies and fleets move on different graphs, so `dp_adjacent()` needs to know
which kind of unit is asking. An army in Paris may walk into Burgundy; a
fleet in Brest may not.

```{r adjacent}
dp_adjacent(board, "par", "army")
dp_adjacent(board, "bre", "fleet")
```

## A new game

`dp_new_game()` sets up Spring 1901 with the canonical 22-unit opening
position and each power owning its home centres.

```{r new-game}
game <- dp_new_game()
game
```

The units are a plain tibble, so anything you would normally do to a data
frame works.

```{r units}
dp_units(game, "France")
```

`dp_power_counts()` is the scoreboard: centres held, units on the board, and
the difference between them, which is what the winter adjustment phase acts
on.

```{r counts}
dp_power_counts(game)
```

## Looking at the board

`dp_plot_map()` draws a schematic board as a **ggplot2** object: seas in
blue, land in buff, supply centres ringed, and each unit as an `A` or an `F`
in its owner's colour. `autoplot()` on a game does the same thing.

```{r plot-opening}
dp_plot_map(game)
```

The palette is colourblind-safe and available on its own as `dp_palette()`,
so charts you build yourself can use the same colours.

## Writing orders

Orders can be written the way players write them. `dp_parse_orders()` reads
standard notation and returns a `dp_orders` tibble.

```{r parse}
french <- dp_parse_orders(c(
  "France: A Par - Bur",
  "France: A Mar - Spa",
  "France: F Bre - Mao"
))
french
```

The same orders can be built programmatically with `dp_order()` and stacked
with `dp_bind_orders()`, which is what you want when orders are generated
rather than typed.

```{r order}
dp_bind_orders(
  dp_order("England", "move", "lon", target = "nth",
           unit_type = "fleet"),
  dp_order("England", "support", "edi", aux = c("lon", "nth"),
           unit_type = "fleet", aux_type = "fleet")
)
```

Unit types are optional. They are only there to make an order readable; the
engine takes the real types from the board when it adjudicates.

If you are not sure what a unit may legally do, ask. `dp_legal_orders()`
enumerates every order the rules allow a power to issue in the current phase,
convoyed moves included.

```{r legal}
legal <- dp_legal_orders(game, "France")
table(legal$type)
```

The full notation reference, including retreats, builds and the coast
qualifiers, lives in `vignette("notation")`.

## Adjudicating a turn

`dp_adjudicate()` resolves a movement phase. It takes the game and the orders
and returns a `dp_result`.

```{r adjudicate}
orders <- dp_example_orders("spring_1901")
result <- dp_adjudicate(game, orders)
result
```

Two orders failed. `summary()` on a result returns the effective orders with
two extra columns: `success`, which says whether the order achieved anything,
and `note`, which says how the engine treated the order in the first place.

```{r failures}
resolved <- summary(result)
resolved[!resolved$success, c("power", "loc", "target", "success", "note")]
```

Both Russia and Turkey ordered a fleet into the Black Sea, neither had
support, and the two attacks cancelled. A province where a move bounced is
recorded as contested, which matters because dislodged units may not retreat
into it.

```{r contested}
result$contested
```

Units that were not ordered, or whose order broke the rules, hold. Nothing is
ever rejected outright: an unparseable order is an error at parse time, but
an order that is merely illegal on the board becomes a hold with a note.

## Advancing the game

A result does not change the game; `dp_advance()` does. It applies the
outcome, steps the season and phase machine, recalculates supply-centre
ownership when the year turns, and checks for a solo victory.

```{r advance}
game <- dp_advance(game, result)
game
```

Nothing was dislodged in the spring, so the retreat phase is skipped and the
game moves straight to the autumn.

## A full year

The autumn works the same way. This time the moves are contested, and the
autumn is the season in which supply centres change hands.

```{r fall}
result <- dp_adjudicate(game, dp_example_orders("fall_1901"))
game <- dp_advance(game, result)
game
```

Ownership has been recalculated on the way into the winter, so several powers
now own more centres than they have units and are owed builds. The winter
adjustment phase is resolved by `dp_build()`.

```{r build}
builds <- dp_parse_orders(
  c("France: Build A Par", "France: Build F Bre", "France: Build F Mar"),
  phase = "build"
)
result <- dp_build(game, builds)
summary(result)[, c("power", "type", "unit_type", "loc", "success", "note")]
```

France ordered three builds and got three. Every other power is owed builds
too but ordered none, which is legal — an unused build is simply forfeited
for the year.

```{r advance-build}
game <- dp_advance(game, result)
game
```

Spring 1902, and the game is ready for the next set of orders. The third
phase type, the retreat phase, is resolved by `dp_retreat()`; it only appears
in years where something was actually dislodged.

## Letting the engine play

Driving the three adjudicators by hand is useful when you care about a
particular position. When you do not, `dp_step()` resolves whatever phase the
game is in and hands back the next state, filling in orders for any power you
did not order with a bot.

```{r step}
mine <- dp_parse_orders(c("France: A Par - Pic", "France: F Bre - Mao"))
dp_step(game, orders = mine, bots = "greedy")
```

Bots stand in for whole powers, not for individual units. France ordered two
of its six units here, so the other four held; the six other powers were
played by the greedy bot.

`dp_play()` runs that loop until someone wins or the turn cap is reached, and
records every turn in a `dp_history`.

```{r play}
history <- dp_play(bots = "hold", max_years = 2, seed = 1)
history
```

The history coerces to a tibble with one row per power per turn, which is the
natural input for a plot or a model.

```{r history-tibble}
head(as_tibble(history), 4)
```

## Where to go next

* `vignette("notation")` — every order form the parser accepts.
* `vignette("adjudication")` — how the engine resolves a turn, worked
  position by worked position.
* `vignette("ai-and-simulation")` — the bots, batch simulation and the
  analysis plots.
* `vignette("design")` — the S3 architecture and why the resolver works the
  way it does.

There is also a **shiny** application bundled with the package. It gives you
the board, an order editor that checks legality as you type, a turn
adjudicator, a replayable history and a simulation runner:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
dp_run_app()
```
